name: Open Source Maintainers
blurb: The people keeping critical AI infrastructure alive.

members.hook: O'Reilly has spent four decades doing the same thing under different names: spotting a technology shift before the industry has language for it, then naming it. 'Open source' and 'Web 2.0' both trace to conferences he convened, and his publishing house has been the technical-literacy backbone for the programmers who built the modern internet, and now AI.
members.name: Tim O'Reilly
members.moniker: Publisher Who Named Web 2.0 and the Open Source Movement

reading.body:
Tim O'Reilly's primary contribution to AI infrastructure is terminological and cultural: he has twice provided the vocabulary that let an industry coordinate around a new paradigm, first with open source and then with Web 2.0, and the programmers trained on O'Reilly publications carried both frameworks into the systems now running AI workloads.

Naming matters in technology because shared language accelerates coordination. When developers agree on what a thing is called, they can build standards, toolchains, and communities around it faster. O'Reilly's four decades of doing this, through conferences and publishing, shaped the open-source norms that govern how AI libraries, frameworks, and model weights are shared and maintained today.

The data covers one person and says nothing about the broader population of open-source maintainers, their funding, their geographic distribution, or the specific projects they sustain. It does not connect O'Reilly's work directly to compute, power, or physical infrastructure. What it documents is narrower: the role of a single person in creating the cultural and linguistic conditions under which open-source AI infrastructure became conceivable as a category at all.
